scenes.title: Files & Directories
scenes.narration: Creating, copying, moving, and deleting files and folders are the everyday building blocks of working at the command line.

scenes.title: The Core Verbs
bullets: mkdir makes new directories to organize your work into logical folders.
touch creates an empty file or updates a file's timestamp instantly.
cp copies files while mv both moves and renames them.
rm deletes files, so it demands a moment of caution every time.
scenes.narration: A handful of verbs cover nearly everything. Use mkdir to carve out folders that keep projects tidy, and touch to spin up an empty file in one keystroke. The cp command duplicates a file, while mv both relocates and renames it depending on where you point it. Finally rm removes files, and because there is no recycle bin here, it deserves respect.

scenes.title: Working with Files
scenes.code:
mkdir project           # make a folder
touch project/notes.txt # create empty file
cp notes.txt backup.txt # copy
mv backup.txt old.txt   # rename
rm old.txt              # delete
scenes.narration: This sequence walks through a full life cycle: we build a folder, drop an empty file inside it, then copy that file to a backup. The mv command renames the backup, and rm removes the file we no longer need. Notice how each command reads almost like plain English once you know the verbs.

scenes.text: rm has no undo and no trash can — double-check the path before you press Enter, and be especially careful with rm -r.
scenes.narration: Deletion at the terminal is permanent, with no trash to rescue you. Always confirm the target path before hitting Enter, particularly with the recursive rm -r flag.
